keyVerseText: When the even was come, they brought unto him many that were possessed with devils: and he cast out the spirits with his word, and healed all that were sick:
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective ὄψιος (ópsios) derives from the adverb ὀψέ (opsé), which means 'late' or 'at evening.' This root emphasizes the time after the close of the day, specifically the latter part of daylight progressing into nightfall. Thus, beyond the simple English gloss of 'evening,' the root sense conveys a sense of lateness or the transition from day to night, highlighting a temporal boundary in daily life.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, ὄψιος appears fifteen times, consistently referring to the evening or late part of the day. It is translated variously as 'when the even,' 'the even,' 'evening,' and 'when even,' demonstrating a stable semantic range centered on the time of day toward nightfall. This consistency in usage underscores the word's function as a temporal marker rather than a metaphorical or symbolic term.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὄψιος as the late evening enriches our grasp of biblical narrative timing and God's sovereign activity within human daily rhythms. The evening often marks moments of transition, rest, and divine intervention, reminding believers that God's power is present even as the day wanes. This temporal marker invites reflection on Christ's ministry extending into all hours, emphasizing His authority over darkness and the unfolding of salvation history. The word roots our faith in the reality of God's presence throughout the full span of our lives, including times of uncertainty or ending.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 8:16 states, 'When the even was come, they brought unto him many that were possessed with devils: and he cast out the spirits with his word, and healed all that were sick.' The use of ὄψιος here highlights that Jesus' healing ministry continued into the late hours of the day, underscoring His tireless compassion and power. The term sets the scene for divine intervention at a time often associated with rest or vulnerability, illustrating that Christ's care transcends normal human schedules and darkness.
